title: Marginal Costing
outcomes: Apply CVP analysis: P/V ratio, break-even, margin of safety and target profit.
Use marginal costing for key factor and other short-term decisions.
Reconcile absorption and marginal costing profits.

meta.exam_tip: If two periods' sales and profits are given, find P/V ratio from the changes first; everything else follows.

concepts.title: Marginal costing and contribution
body: Marginal costing charges only variable costs to products; fixed costs are treated as period costs and written off in full against contribution.
Contribution = sales − variable cost; it first covers fixed costs and then gives profit. Profit = contribution − fixed costs.
Marginal cost is the change in total cost from producing one more unit; in practice it equals variable cost per unit. Stocks are valued at variable cost under marginal costing.
concepts.analogy: Each unit sold adds its contribution to a pot that pays fixed costs first and then becomes profit.
concepts.work: If a pen sells for ₹20 with variable cost ₹12, each pen contributes ₹8 towards fixed costs.

concepts.title: Cost-volume-profit analysis
body: P/V ratio = contribution ÷ sales × 100; it also equals change in profit ÷ change in sales.
Break-even point (units) = fixed cost ÷ contribution per unit; (sales) = fixed cost ÷ P/V ratio.
Margin of safety = actual sales − break-even sales; profit = margin of safety × P/V ratio. Sales for a target profit = (fixed cost + target profit) ÷ P/V ratio.

Assumptions: costs divide cleanly into fixed and variable; selling price and variable cost per unit are constant; one product or a constant mix; no change in stock levels. A break-even chart and a profit-volume graph show these relations visually; the angle of incidence reflects the profit-earning rate.
concepts.analogy: CVP answers "how much must we sell" questions with three numbers: fixed cost, contribution and sales.
concepts.work: Two periods with sales ₹10 lakh and ₹12 lakh and profits ₹1 lakh and ₹1.6 lakh give P/V ratio 30%.

concepts.title: Decisions using marginal costing
body: Key (limiting) factor: when a resource is scarce, rank products by contribution per unit of that factor, not by contribution per unit.
Make or buy: buy if the purchase price is less than the variable cost of making (plus any avoidable fixed cost), considering capacity use.

Accept a special order below normal price if it covers variable cost, does not displace regular sales and spare capacity exists. Shut down temporarily if contribution does not cover avoidable fixed costs (shutdown point = avoidable fixed cost ÷ contribution per unit).
Other uses: pricing in recession, choosing between alternatives, and evaluating discounts.
concepts.analogy: Short-term decisions turn on contribution, because fixed costs often stay unchanged.
concepts.work: An order at ₹70 for a product with variable cost ₹60 adds ₹10 per unit if there is idle capacity.

concepts.title: Absorption versus marginal costing
body: Absorption costing includes fixed production overheads in product cost and stock; marginal costing does not.

When production exceeds sales (stock increases), absorption profit is higher, because part of fixed overhead is carried in closing stock; when sales exceed production, marginal profit is higher; when equal, both profits match.
Difference in profit = change in stock units × fixed overhead per unit.
concepts.analogy: The two methods differ only in when fixed production overhead hits profit.
concepts.work: Producing 10,000 and selling 8,000 with fixed overhead of ₹20 a unit makes absorption profit ₹40,000 higher.

illustrations.title: Break-even and beyond
illustrations.q: A product sells at ₹100; variable cost ₹60; fixed costs ₹4,00,000 a year; current sales 15,000 units. Compute P/V ratio, break-even units and sales, profit, margin of safety, and units needed for a profit of ₹3,00,000.

solution.text: Check: profit = margin of safety sales × P/V ratio = ₹5,00,000 × 40% = ₹2,00,000.

illustrations.title: Too few machine hours
illustrations.q: Machine hours are limited to 10,000. Product A: contribution ₹60/unit, 4 hours/unit, demand 2,000 units. Product B: contribution ₹50/unit, 2 hours/unit, demand 3,000 units. Find the best product mix and contribution.

solution.text: Total contribution ₹2,10,000. Ranking by contribution per unit (A first) would give less.

jobs.title: Special order evaluation
jobs.situation: An export buyer offers ₹75 per unit for 5,000 units; normal price ₹100, variable cost ₹62.
jobs.takeaway: With spare capacity, any price above variable cost adds profit.

mcqs.explain: Contribution covers fixed costs and then gives profit. In practice: compute per unit and in total.

mcqs.q: Fixed cost ₹3,00,000; P/V ratio 25%. Break-even sales:
mcqs.explain: 3,00,000 ÷ 25% = 12,00,000. In practice: use for sales targets.

mcqs.q: Sales ₹8,00,000; profit ₹80,000; P/V ratio 40%. Margin of safety:
mcqs.explain: MOS = profit ÷ P/V = 80,000 ÷ 40% = 2,00,000. In practice: 25% of sales.

mcqs.q: Sales ₹5 lakh, profit ₹50,000; sales ₹7 lakh, profit ₹1,10,000. P/V ratio:
mcqs.explain: Change in profit 60,000 ÷ change in sales 2,00,000 = 30%. In practice: fixed cost = 1,50,000 − 50,000 = 1,00,000.

mcqs.q: With a scarce resource, products are ranked by:
options: Contribution per unit of the scarce resource
mcqs.explain: The key factor rule maximises total contribution. In practice: also meet minimum demand commitments.

mcqs.q: A component costs ₹45 to buy; variable cost to make ₹40; fixed costs unaffected. Decision:
mcqs.explain: Making saves ₹5 a unit since fixed costs do not change. In practice: consider capacity for other products.

mcqs.q: When closing stock exceeds opening stock, absorption profit is:
mcqs.explain: Fixed overhead carried forward in stock reduces absorption costing's period charge. In practice: difference = stock change × fixed OH per unit.

mcqs.q: Under marginal costing, closing stock is valued at:
mcqs.explain: Only variable production costs are inventoried. In practice: financial reporting needs absorption cost.

questions.q: A product sells at ₹100; variable cost ₹60; fixed costs ₹4,00,000 a year; current sales 15,000 units. Compute P/V ratio, break-even units and sales, profit, margin of safety, and units needed for a profit of ₹3,00,000.

model.text: Check: profit = margin of safety sales × P/V ratio = ₹5,00,000 × 40% = ₹2,00,000.

mistakes: Dividing fixed cost by selling price.

questions.q: Machine hours are limited to 10,000. Product A: contribution ₹60/unit, 4 hours/unit, demand 2,000 units. Product B: contribution ₹50/unit, 2 hours/unit, demand 3,000 units. Find the best product mix and contribution.

model.text: Total contribution ₹2,10,000. Ranking by contribution per unit (A first) would give less.

summary: Contribution = sales − variable cost; profit = contribution − fixed cost.
P/V = C/S; BEP = F ÷ C per unit or F ÷ P/V.
MOS = sales − BEP sales; profit = MOS × P/V.
Key factor: rank by contribution per unit of scarce resource.
Absorption vs marginal: stock change × fixed OH per unit.
traps: Do not rank by contribution per unit when a resource is limited.

viva.model: A technique that charges only variable costs to products and treats fixed costs as period costs written off against contribution.

viva.q: How is the break-even point found?
viva.model: By dividing fixed costs by contribution per unit for units, or by the P/V ratio for sales value.
The excess of actual or budgeted sales over break-even sales; profit equals margin of safety times P/V ratio.
A resource in short supply that limits output, such as machine hours or materials, used to rank products by contribution per unit of it.

viva.q: Why do absorption and marginal profits differ?
viva.model: Because absorption costing carries fixed production overhead in stock, so profit differs by the change in stock times fixed overhead per unit.

cases.title: Bright Lamps
cases.case: Bright Lamps: price ₹500, variable cost ₹300 per lamp, fixed costs ₹6,00,000. Expected sales 4,500 lamps. A retailer offers to buy 500 extra lamps at ₹350; capacity is 6,000 lamps.

mcqs.explain: 6,00,000 ÷ 200 = 3,000. In practice: sales of 4,500 give comfortable cover.

mcqs.q: Extra profit from the special order:
mcqs.explain: 500 × (350 − 300) = 25,000 with spare capacity and no extra fixed cost. In practice: protect regular prices.
